checks.invariant: After DELETE /sandboxes/{sid} returns, no agent pre-destructive snapshot is recorded for the deleted sandbox and no snapshot image is left behind (delete_sandbox vs call_tool -> _snapshot, which holds only _snap_locks, not _lifecycle).
checks.result: Deterministic schedule with real AgentBox/AuditLog/ApprovalStore/SandboxManager code (sqlite in scratch) and a fake Docker client whose commit blocks until released: agent call_tool(write/delete_file) entered SandboxManager.snapshot (status check via _container at sandbox.py:351 passed, commit at :355 in progress); human delete_sandbox ran and returned (status=deleted, snapshot_rows=[], images=[]). When the commit then completed, sandbox.py:358-362 inserted snapshot row snap_6a3f7373 for the deleted sandbox, the image agentbox-snap:sb_1-snap_6a3f7373 remained in the (fake) daemon, and the audit log shows system 'snapshot' (id 4) after human 'sandbox_delete' (id 3), then tool_error 'deleted sandbox'. A second DELETE on the deleted id removes the orphan (sandboxes.delete has no deleted-status guard), but nothing triggers it. Whether real dockerd lets an in-flight commit finish while 'rm -f' removes the container is not established locally -> needs_validation.

checks.invariant: After restore returns, no agent/approved/human-import action writes to or snapshots the old container, and snapshot rows are attributed correctly.
checks.result: No container identity is carried from check to use: _snapshot (service.py:261-276), _run_tool (service.py:129-161) and sandbox tool methods re-resolve container_id from the DB per call (_container sandbox.py:225-232, _require_running :343-347). An in-flight exec/write that already resolved the old container hits it before removal (harmless, state discarded) or fails with a docker NotFound/APIError; one resolved after restore's UPDATE (sandbox.py:401-403) runs on the restored container, which the agent may do anyway with its still-valid token. Snapshot rows carry only sandbox_id (sandbox.py:63-69), so a commit of the old container completing across restore is correctly attributed to sid and is listable/removable by later delete. Variant gap (hardening, not a boundary result): the pre-destructive snapshot taken for an in-flight write/decide/import_file may be of the old container rather than the restored state being overwritten; the overwritten content still exists in the restore-source snapshot. Pending approvals survive restore (restore_sandbox service.py:528-536 does not expire them) and execute on the restored container with a preview/capture computed on the old one; the agent can already change files between preview and approval, so restore adds no agent advantage.

checks.invariant: GUI bursts are never bound to a container other than the one the covered GUI input runs on, across restore.
checks.result: GuiBursts.open (gui_bursts.py:73-87) takes no burst lock and is not fenced by _lifecycle. Schedule: agent GUI input is inside _snapshot's commit (service.py:264) when restore_sandbox runs end_desktop -> bursts.end (finds no burst; _snapshot closed it at :263); open then reads the old container_id and baseline from the old container before restore removes it (sandbox.py:395); restore installs the new container and reset_timers; the input's _run_tool (service.py:141-150) passes covers() (gui_bursts.py:68-71 checks only sid in _gui_burst, not container_id) and clicks on the restored container. That single input is covered by a burst whose close reports gui_burst_close_failed 'container replaced' (gui_bursts.py:132-136; intended per tests/test_m2_unit.py:247-257) with no stray kill or gui_changes, and the next burst's baseline includes what it started. Reach of one input on a freshly reset desktop is minimal and the window is narrow (open must finish between end_desktop and the docker remove), so recorded as hardening, not a candidate. Restore that closes a burst opened earlier is fail-closed (end closes it; covers() then refuses).

checks.invariant: A lifecycle call cannot be deadlocked or starved by tool calls, takeover or burst close holding _snap_locks, gui_lock, burst locks or concurrency slots, and _life_locks does not grow without bound from a lower-trust principal.
checks.result: Lock order inside _lifecycle (service.py:499-504): life -> audit lock (log_human) -> burst lock (end -> close, gui_bursts.py:117-128) -> gui_lock via handback's _gui_locked with a 30 s timeout whose ServiceError end_desktop swallows (service.py:647-655). No tool, decide, takeover or burst path ever takes _life_locks, and lifecycle never takes _snap_locks or _busy, so no cycle exists. The agent can delay a lifecycle call only by a burst close in progress (bounded by _timed X and manifest execs, sandbox.py:376 30 s) or by holding gui_lock (bounded by GUI_LOCK_WAIT=30); new closes need new bursts, which need quota-limited snapshots. All lifecycle routes are human_only/browser_human (api.py:248-269, web.py:270-287), so _life_locks keys (created before any existence check, service.py:502) come only from the human principal; _snap_locks/_busy keys are created per authenticated call, and an agent is fixed to its own sid. Growth is human-driven only: hardening.

checks.invariant: Every SandboxManager method that snapshots, resumes, pauses or execs refuses a deleted sandbox.
checks.result: restore checks deleted explicitly (sandbox.py:389) and re-checks with a conditional UPDATE (:401-406). snapshot, pause, resume, workspace_manifest go through _container (sandbox.py:225-228, deleted -> SandboxError); exec/list_dir/read/write/delete/upload/is_dir/outbox and desktop tools go through _require_running/_desktop -> _container (sandbox.py:343-347, sandbox_desktop.py:64-67). delete has no guard, which keeps it idempotent. The guards are check-then-act: a status check passed before a concurrent delete does not stop the in-flight docker call, so the commit race in check 1 is the remaining gap.

candidates.title: Agent pre-write snapshot that is still committing when the human deletes the sandbox leaves an untracked snapshot image and a snapshot record for the deleted sandbox
candidates.description: delete_sandbox holds only the per-sandbox _lifecycle lock. The agent's automatic snapshot before a destructive tool (call_tool -> _call_tool -> _snapshot, holding only _snap_locks), the approved-run snapshot in decide, and the import_file snapshot never take that lock. SandboxManager.snapshot checks the deleted status once in _container, then runs a multi-second docker commit, then inserts the snapshot row without checking status again. If the human's DELETE runs during the commit, delete removes the container, marks the sandbox deleted and removes the snapshot images it can list, then returns. The commit then finishes: a snapshot row is inserted for the deleted sandbox, the system writes a 'snapshot' audit row after 'sandbox_delete', and the committed image (the agent's whole writable layer, which the agent can make large with many write_file calls) stays on the host Docker disk. Nothing removes it unless someone issues DELETE again for the already-deleted id, and the UI hides deleted sandboxes. A sandboxed schedule with real agentbox code and a fake Docker client reproduced this end to end. The one fact not established here is whether real dockerd lets an in-flight commit finish while 'docker rm -f' removes the container.
candidates.claimed_root_cause: Snapshot creation is check-then-act on the sandbox status (sandbox.py:351 _container check, :355 commit, :358-362 unconditional INSERT) and is not serialised with delete_sandbox (service.py:538-543 under _lifecycle only). SandboxManager.delete (sandbox.py:320-332) cleans up only the snapshot rows that exist when it runs list_snapshots, so a commit that completes after that point is never cleaned up.

trace.description: Agent calls write_file on an existing path (allowed by default policy, which snapshots on overwrite) or another SNAPSHOT_TOOLS tool; runs on tool_pool via box.call_tool.
Takes the per-sandbox _snap_locks lock (not _lifecycle) and enters _call_tool.
The allow path with _needs_snapshot true calls _snapshot before running the tool (decide at service.py:467 and import_file at :555 reach the same call).
_container checks status != deleted once and returns the container handle.

A multi-second docker commit runs. Meanwhile the human DELETE runs delete_sandbox -> SandboxManager.delete: removes the container (:323), sets status deleted (:326), and removes the images of the snapshot rows that exist so far (:328-332).

After the commit returns, the snapshot row is inserted for the deleted sandbox with no status re-check. Its image is never removed, and _snapshot (service.py:269) appends a 'snapshot' audit record after the delete.

evidence.description: _lifecycle is the only per-sandbox serialisation for delete; call_tool, decide and import_file never acquire it.
delete removes only the images of snapshot rows that exist when list_snapshots runs.
The snapshot INSERT runs after the commit with no deleted-status check, unlike restore's conditional UPDATE at sandbox.py:401-406.
_snapshot writes the 'snapshot' audit row for the sandbox regardless of its current status.

blockers: Real Docker 29.9.1 behaviour is not observable in the sandbox (no Docker socket). The local check assumed that a 'docker commit' already in progress (pause=True) completes and keeps its image when the same container is force-removed concurrently (container rm -f during commit). If dockerd instead fails the commit, or blocks the remove until the commit ends and the remove still lands before the INSERT, the orphan does not occur in practice.
Local harness output (agents/h-lifecycle/artifacts/h.out) uses a fake Docker client. It shows the agentbox-side logic only.

validation_plan.local: Parent-live, disposable loopback setup with a dummy human token: run 'agentbox serve' with the cli template and default policy, then create a sandbox. With the agent token, write /workspace/a.txt, then write many new 8 MiB files with write_file (about 1-2 GiB total, no snapshots) so that the commit takes several seconds. Start POST /sandboxes/{sid}/tools/write_file {path:/workspace/a.txt, content:'x'} with the agent token. About 0.5 s later, while 'docker ps' shows the container paused by the commit, send DELETE /sandboxes/{sid} with the human token and wait for both to return. Observe the result in three places: (1) 'docker images agentbox-snap --filter label=agentbox.sandbox=<sid>' lists an image after DELETE returned 204; (2) sqlite 'SELECT * FROM snapshots WHERE sandbox_id=<sid>' has a row while sandboxes.status='deleted'; (3) GET /audit shows a system 'snapshot' event after human 'sandbox_delete'. Repeat with delays of 0.1, 0.5 and 2 s. Then clean up by sending DELETE again (which removes the orphan) and running 'docker image rm'.

hardening: service.py covers()/GuiBursts.covers (gui_bursts.py:68-71) checks only that a burst exists, not that burst['container_id'] equals the current sandboxes.get(sid)['container_id']. A GUI input whose burst was opened on the pre-restore container (open at gui_bursts.py:73-87 races restore_sandbox between end_desktop and the docker remove) can run on the restored container with no stray kill or gui_changes, and what it starts joins the next baseline. Fix: compare container ids in covers() and refuse with the same F2 message. Regression: open a burst with container_id c1, set the current container to c2, then call _run_tool click; expect a SandboxError and no click.

restore_sandbox (service.py:528-536) and delete_sandbox (service.py:538-543) do not expire pending approvals for the sandbox. After a restore, an approval whose preview and capture were computed on the abandoned container can still be approved and runs on the restored container. Suggest claiming them as EXPIRED (with a reason such as 'sandbox_restored'/'sandbox_deleted') inside the lifecycle lock.

Lifecycle calls do not fence in-flight tool, decide or import calls: an action queued behind _snap_locks or in preview during restore runs on the restored container, but its AP-2 pre-destructive snapshot may be of the old container. Suggest a per-sandbox generation (or container_id) captured at call_tool/decide entry and re-checked before _run_tool, or having lifecycle methods acquire _snap_locks for the sid.

pause_sandbox (service.py:506-511) does not serialise with an agent docker commit (pause=True). Depending on dockerd, the human pause may fail with an unmapped docker APIError (HTTP 500), or the commit's deferred unpause may resume a container that the DB records as paused. Suggest taking _snap_locks in pause/resume, or verifying the container state after pause.

_life_locks (service.py:90, created at :502 before any existence check), _snap_locks (:296) and _busy (:290) keep one entry per sid string forever. Keys come only from human-authenticated lifecycle routes or from callers authenticated to the sid, so growth is human-driven only. Suggest pruning entries on delete and validating that the sid exists before setdefault.

SandboxManager.exec/upload/_write_chunks pass docker NotFound/APIError (for example, an exec on a container that restore or delete just removed) through as non-SandboxError exceptions. The caller gets HTTP 500 and no tool_error audit row. Suggest mapping docker.errors.APIError to SandboxError in the tool methods.
